body.text: Few places or corridors tell a richer story of geography and human movement than Uttarakhand. Stepping into its history reveals how trade, terrain, and culture shaped the modern map.

Uttarakhand, also known as Uttaranchal (English:, the official name until 2007), is a state in northern India that is bordered by Himachal Pradesh to the north-west, Tibet to the north, Nepal to the east and Uttar Pradesh to the south. 6% of the area of India.

The state's winter capital is Dehradun, its summer capital is Bhararisain and its judicial capital is Nainital. The state's two divisions, Garhwal and Kumaon, are subdivided into a total of 13 districts. 4% of the state's geographical area and 16% of the land is cultivatable.

The state's two major rivers, the Ganges and its tributary the Yamuna, originate in the Gangotri and Yamunotri glaciers, respectively. Utterakhand is sixth among the Top 10 Greenest States in India with Best AQI.

Archaeological evidence shows Uttarakhand has been inhabited since prehistoric times. During the Vedic period, it was part of the ancient Kuru and the Panchal kingdoms, and later saw the rise of dynasties like the Kunindas and the influence of Buddhism, as evidenced by Ashokan edicts.
The states economy, whilst mainly driven by agriculture and hydropower, is now dominated by the service industry, mostly travel, tourism, and the hotel industry. 9 trillion or US$42 billion in 2026).
The state contributes five seats to the Council of States (Lok Sabha) and three seats to the House of the People (Rajya Sabha) of the Parliament of India.

Inhabitants of Uttarakhand are called either Garhwali or Kumaoni, depending on their region of origin. Hinduism is practised by more than three-quarters of the population, with Islam being the next-largest religious group.

Hindi is the most-widely spoken language and is the official language of the state, along with regional languages, including Garhwali, Jaunsari, Rongpo, Bhotia, Gurjari and Kumaoni. The state is often referred to as the "Devabhumi" (lit. 'Land of the Gods'), due to its religious significance, and numerous Hindu temples and pilgrimage centres.
The states historical, natural and religious tourist destinations, include Char Dham, Haridwar, Rishikesh, Panch Kedar, the Himalayas and Sapta Badri, and two World Heritage sites.
Etymology

Uttarakhand's name is derived from the Sanskrit words uttara (उत्तर) meaning 'north', and khaṇḍa (खण्ड) meaning 'section' or 'part', altogether meaning 'Northern Part'. The name is mentioned in early Hindu scriptures as the combined region of "Kedarkhand" (present day Garhwal) and "Manaskhand" (present day Kumaon).
"Uttarakhand" is also the ancient Puranic term for the central stretch of the Indian Himalayas.
History

Archaeological evidence supports the existence of humans in the region since prehistoric times. Though initially, it was thought the region was uninhabited due to its harsh climate and mountainous terrain, excavations and the study of ancient literature, established that the region has been inhabited by humans since the Stone Age.

Evidence of Stone-Age settlements has been found in parts of Kumaon and Garhwal, notably at rock shelters at Lakhudyar, Almora. Ancient rock paintings, rock shelters, paleolithic age stone tools, and megaliths provide evidence that the mountains of the region have been inhabited since prehistoric times. Later archaeological remains show the existence of early Vedic (c.

The Pauravas, Khasas, Kiratas, Nandas, Mauryas, Kushanas, Kunindas, Guptas, Karkotas, Palas, Gurjara-Pratiharas, Katyuris, Raikas, Chands, Parmars or Panwars, Mallas, Shahs and the British have ruled Uttarakhand in turns.

The region formed a part of the Uttarakuru Kingdom during the Vedic period of Ancient India. Among the first major dynasties of Kumaon were the Kunindas in the second century BCE who practised an early form of Shaivism. Ashokan edicts at Kalsi show the early presence of Buddhism in this region.

Among the first major dynasties of Garhwal and Kumaon in the second century BCE were the Kunindas, who practised an early form of Shaivism and traded salt with western Tibet. The Ashokan edict at Kalsi in Western Garhwal records evidence of Buddhism in this region. Shamanic Hindu practices deviating from Hindu orthodoxy also persisted here.
Garhwal and Kumaon were restored to nominal Vedic Hindu rule due to the travels of Shankaracharya and the arrival of migrants from the plains.

Between the 4th and 14th centuries, the Katyuri dynasty dominated lands in the Katyur valley (modern-day Baijnath) in Kumaon. The Katyuris built historically significant temples at Jageshwar that were later remodelled by the Chands.

Other peoples of the Tibeto-Burman group known as Kirata settled in the northern highlands and in other parts of the region, and are believed to be ancestors of the modern-day Bhotiya, Raji, Jad and Banrawat peoples.

During the medieval period, the region was consolidated under the Katyuri rulers of Kumaon, also known as the Kurmanchal Kingdom. After the fall of Katyuris, the region was divided into the Kumaon Kingdom and the Garhwal Kingdom.

By the medieval period, the region was consolidated under the Garhwal Kingdom in the west and the Kumaon Kingdom in the east. During this period, learning and new forms of painting (the Pahari school of art) developed.

Modern-day Garhwal was likewise unified under the rule of Parmars who, along with many other Rajputs and Brahmins, also arrived from the plains. The Timli estate founded in Dehradun mid-15th century by Chaudhari Ram Singh, a member of the Chokar Hindu family, remained under the rule of this dynasty until its eventual annexation.

In 1548, two chieftains, Pohda Singh and Lal Karan, from the Titron region in Saharanpur district, crossed the Sivalik Hills, conquered the entire Dehradun area, and established the Timli estate. They founded a town named Timli, in which Chaudhari Bhagwan Singh had the power of magistrate.

In 1791, the expanding Gorkha Empire of Nepal overran Almora, the seat of the Kumaon Kingdom. It was annexed to the Kingdom of Nepal by Amar Singh Thapa. In 1803, the Garhwal Kingdom also fell to the Gurkhas.

After the Anglo-Nepalese War, this region was ceded to the British as part of the Treaty of Sugauli and the erstwhile Kumaon Kingdom along with the eastern region of Garhwal Kingdom was merged with the Ceded and Conquered Provinces.
In 1816, the Garhwal Kingdom was re-established from a smaller region in Tehri as a princely state.

In southern Uttarakhand, in Haridwar district (part of Saharanpur until 1988), some local Hindu rulers exercised dominance and kingship (rajya). The area was under the control of Parmar (Panwar) chiefs in eastern Saharanpur, including Haridwar, in the reign of Raja Sabha Chandra of Jabarhera (Jhabrera).

The Panwar clan held more than 500 villages in upper Doab this situation was confirmed in 1759 in a grant by a Rohilla governor of 505 villages and 31 hamlets to Manohar Singh, written in some records as Raja Nahar Singh son of Sabha Chandra.

In 1792, Ram Dayal and his son Sawai Singh ruled the area, but Ramdayal left Jhabrera and went to Landhaura village. Some villages were under the control of Raja Ramdayal Singh at Landhaura, and some under his son Sawai Singh at Jhabrera.

Hence, there were two branches of Jhabrera State (riyasat) main branch at Jhabrera and a second at Landhaura, both father and son ruled simultaneously without any conflicts until the death of Raja Sawai Singh of Jabarhera in 1803.
After the death of Sawai Singh, total control of powers transferred to Ram Dayal Singh at Landhaura, but some villages were given to descendants of Sawai Singh and her widow to collect revenue.
Colonial era

By 1803, there were 794 Landhaura villages under Raja Ram Dayal Singh, who died on 29 March 1813. The British originally recognised these holdings, at least those in the original grant made by the Rohilla governor, in land settlements concluded with Ram Dayal and his heirs.

Later, more settlements appear to have been made with the village communities, and by 1850, little of the once-vast estate of the Landhaura Khübars remained. The Rajas of Landhaura built many temples and Ghats on the Ganga river, therefore they are also famous as the Haridwari Rajas in folk history and literature.
The Dakshamahadev Temple at Kankhal was built by Queen DhanKaur of Landhaura in 1810.
Raja Ranjit Singh of Samthar state, born in 1943, was married at a young age to a princess from the Chokar family, which ruled the Timli estate in Dehradun.
